newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand says IMF package likely soon.
newsitem.headline: Thailand says IMF package likely soon.

text.p: Thailand is still talking with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) but the framework of a rescue package is expected to be worked out and approved by the cabinet this week, the finance minister said on Monday.
The minister, Thanong Bidaya, told a news conference no loan details had been worked out but he would seek cabinet approval for the basic framework of the IMF package on Tuesday.
"Discussions have been going well and the key policy elements of such a package are falling in place," he said.
"Work will continue to develop and all details of a comprehensive programme finalised as expeditiously as possible."
Thanong was due to explain the package on Tuesday in a nationally-televised address.

He told the news conference financial officials had worked for a week with a team from the IMF to try to assess the economic situation in order to develop measures to stabilise the economy and lay the basis for restoring sustainable growth.
He said the cabinet must approve the measures, and the IMF would also send the package to its board for approval.
Thanong, haggard after seven days of talks with the IMF team, disagreed with a reporter who commented that he looked sad.
"You call this face sad? I'm smiling," he said. "I am confident it's going to be approved by the cabinet and it's going to be good news."
Thanong did not comment on reports that Japan would provide loans through the Export-Import Bank of Japan in cooperation with the IMF.
Japanese government sources said Tokyo would decide on a financial support package for Thailand within the next two weeks.

The Japanese financial newspaper Nihon Keizai Shimbun said on Sunday the Export-Import Bank of Japan and the IMF had put together an $8 billion emergency loan package for Thailand to boost the economy.
Japan's private banks would coordinate several billion dollars in additional loans to help Bangkok shore up its foreign reserves and restructure its economy, the paper said.

Thai finance ministry sources said the conditions prescribed by the IMF would include further large cuts to the government budget, a value-added tax increase, a high interest rate policy at least until the end of the year, and a cut in the government's risk exposure to the finance and property sectors.
They said if these conditions were met, Thailand would have access to the IMF's facilities.
Thailand faces its worst economic crisis in decades following an economic boom that saw heavy overseas borrowing and misallocation of resources to non-productive areas such as the property sector.
Financial institutions have been hit hard by a liquidity crunch and rising non-performing loans.

Thailand's foreign currency debt totals almost $90 billion, about three-quarters of which is to the private sector. Nearly $40 billion of that debt is short term and comes due before the end of the year.
Analysts say there are concerns in the government that creditors may not roll over debt due to a lack of confidence in the government's ability to implement tough measures to boost the economy.
